Well, the biggest reason to move away from anything _buntu is to get away from Canonical and the UCC. They're essentially the same company (Canonical) and they're for profit. Canonical likes to "push" ads to the Ubuntu system, collect user data for profit, and not (openly) give earned money to the other _buntu distros.

I couldn't outline all of the reasons to abandon Canonical, even if I had a week.

Beyond that, I wonder why you're looking at Fedora, specifically. Honestly, I have never had a good time with RHEL-type distros. When I was younger, I tried my damned-est to get The Beefy Miracle on my machines, and failed... I have never tried so hard to fail. That trend has carried through to last month, when I tried to get CentOS on my home server and the install failed.

I can install Gentoo, Arch, and any other distro on any machine, with the exception of RedHat distros. They're just needlessly frustrating (to me) and not geared for daily use.

The Beefy Miracle failed, just because of the release, I think... I heard that a lot of people had problems, and so I blame Fedora. I put so much time into trying to install it, and I tried so many computers, and none of them worked. In the end, I just go up and moved on to something else.

This latest install of CentOS (on my home server) failed because of the way CentOS partitions, I think. I was trying to do LUKS on LVM, which I've done on every install for the last year and a half, and I don't think CentOS was creating the boot partition correctly. Since the distro ONLY let's me work with partitioning and encryption through the GUI, I couldn't change whatever was wrong... I tried the different "options" given to me through the installer, but I could never get it to boot. Ultimately, I gave up and put Debian on the thing, which let me control the partitioning the way I wanted to.

I've installed 3 months ago Fedora in my laptop to replace a Windows Vista. The installer only wanted to know a) my language, b) the partition schema and c) if it was a workstation or a server. And that only because I didn't want the default settings. An hour later my system was ready to work.

That being said, it's the same for the Ubuntus or SUSEs I've installed in other machines. After working in some different distros I find them basically the same thing while installing and very close in daily usage.
I'm sure I can get it t work with default settings... The problem is that I want more from my Linux experience, and RH-based distros don't let you configure things the way other distros will.

In enterprise RedHat based distributions are given preference. If you are intending to learn a system that may help you in future work a Red Hat based system (Fedora, CentOS, RHEL) is the way to go.

Also, Red Hat now gives out one free workstation license for you to run at home. (See the developer program).

I say this as I have seen it over and over in multiple companies and offices. If you want to "Run Linux" It is typically going to be either Red Hat or SUSE. I have seen Red Hat a lot more. SUSE seems to pop up in old novell shops.

Hope that helps.

The only people I've seen really running Fedora as a daily driver are Red Hat employees. I know some people that have kick-around machines that use it, and I load it from time to time just to see what they've changed on the razor's edge of RHEL, but serious workstation use... nobody outside of sales engineers and such.

I have never worked for Red Hat and I use it as a daily driver, and it has been the primary choice since Fedora Core 4. My brother-in-law installed it for me over a decade ago because it is what he uses.

I'm a Fedora user, have been for over a decade. Besides a year or so when Fedora was really not putting out some stable stuff for my hardware at the time, it has been my go to for both desktop and server.

For the most part, they are a wash when it comes to comparing them. There are caveats to each and pros/cons/ depending on your situation. I do web development and I found that some packages (at least for a while) were more up-to-date with Fedora than with Ubuntu (or it's derivatives) such as Nginx, MariaDB (which is default in Fedora), Redis, Python, and PHP. For things like NodeJS and Ruby, I just used the (nvm|rvm) installers to jump between versions as needed on projects.

Before someone brings up the "just use CentOS", it doesn't have the latest versions of packages that I want, specifically PHP 7. Yes I can get it with additional repos, but it's easier to just use Fedora for my situation.

That's my two cents.
